label: Confirmed Cases (2026 DRC + Uganda + France)
source: ECDC Ebola outbreak tracker (published 15 September) — data as of 13 September 2026
contestNote: ECDC's tracker, updated 15 September with data through 13 September, put the national toll at 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths — up from 7,200 cases and 3,475 deaths in the prior (12 September) report. DRC Health Minister Dr. Roger Samuel Kamba said the slowing daily pace (deaths down from ~50 to ~30/day, new infections down from ~120 to ~80/day, and 10 of 62 health zones with no new case for 22+ days) is 'a positive signal' that the response 'is beginning to bend the transmission curve.' But UN Special Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis and WHO's Dr. Olivier le Polain pushed back the same day (15 September), cautioning it is 'too early to confidently say we have passed a peak' given continued growth in North Kivu and Haut-Uélé. Africa CDC separately warned 22 August that the true case count may be 2-3x higher (10,000-15,000) given official detection captures an estimated 30-40% of infections, and that transmission may have begun as early as February 2026, months before the 15 May declaration.
deltaNote: DRC confirmed cases roughly nineteenfold since early June: 400 (June 5) → 2,011 (July 15) → 3,605 (July 30) → 4,053 (August 5) → 4,665 (August 13) → 4,945 (August 16) → 5,021 (August 18) → 5,290 (August 20) → 5,584 (August 23) → 5,713 (August 25) → 5,794 (August 27) → 6,041 (August 31) → 6,186 (August 31 report, published 2 September) → 6,342 (2 September report, published 4 September) → 6,604 (5 September report, published 6 September) → 6,757 (7 September report, published 9 September) → 6,942 (9 September report, published 10 September; ECDC) → 7,022 (10 September report, published 12 September; DRC MoH/AFP) → 7,200 (12 September report, published 13-14 September; DRC/ECDC) → 7,258 (13 September report, published 15 September; ECDC). This is now the largest Ebola outbreak in DRC history and the second-largest ever recorded worldwide, behind only the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic (28,616 cases). WHO's 100-day assessment (24 August) recorded an average of nearly 90 new confirmed cases per day over the outbreak's first three months. A WHO Geneva briefing on 8 September said the response needs 1,600 more treatment beds (target 3,000 across existing ETCs, versus ~1,400 built) and 5,000 more health workers (target 9,000 at 3 staff per bed, versus ~4,000 currently deployed).

label: Lab-Confirmed Cases (2026 Outbreak — DRC + Uganda + France)
source: ECDC Ebola outbreak tracker (published 15 September) — data as of 13 September 2026

deltaNote: 1,726 cumulative recoveries and 905 patients currently hospitalized in isolation as of the 13 September update. label: Deaths (2026 Outbreak)
source: ECDC Ebola outbreak tracker (published 15 September) — data as of 13 September 2026
contestNote: Confirmed deaths: 3,510 DRC + 2 Uganda = 3,512 total as of 13 September (ECDC, published 15 September), a crude CFR of roughly 48.3%. The toll continues climbing, having already surpassed the 2,299 deaths of DRC's 2018-2020 Kivu outbreak to become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history, and per AP reporting is tracking toward surpassing the 11,310-death toll of the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic. DRC Health Minister Roger Samuel Kamba pointed to daily deaths declining from roughly 50 to roughly 30 per day as 'a positive signal,' but UN Special Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said 15 September 'it remains a deadly and a massive epidemic... in other areas, we continue to see growth in cases,' and WHO's Olivier le Polain said it is 'too early to confidently say we have passed a peak.' WHO's 100-day review found roughly 60% of weekly deaths recorded in the prior six weeks occurred in communities outside treatment centers; Tedros warned 2 September that up to 80% of new cases fall outside known contact lists. A 23-year-old man became the first confirmed death in Sud-Ubangi province (western DRC) on 9 September after an extensive cross-country journey through Rwanda and Uganda.
deltaNote: DRC confirmed deaths: 64 (June 5) → 754 (July 15) → 1,587 (July 30) → 1,850 (August 5) → 2,184 (August 13) → 2,325 (August 16) → 2,378 (August 18) → 2,516 (August 20) → 2,680 (August 23) → 2,744 (August 25) → 2,786 (August 27) → 2,911 (August 31) → 3,007 (August 31 report, published 2 September) → 3,072 (2 September report, published 4 September) → 3,175 (5 September report, published 6 September) → 3,267 (7 September report, published 9 September) → 3,349 (9 September report, published 10 September; ECDC) → 3,398 (10 September report, published 12 September; DRC MoH/AFP) → 3,475 (12 September report, published 13-14 September; DRC/ECDC) → 3,510 (13 September report, published 15 September; ECDC). Over 40 healthcare workers killed and treatment centers/ambulances attacked per UN Secretary-General Guterres's 27 August Security Council briefing; a North Kivu community threatened 4 September to burn down a treatment center under construction in Katwa.

label: Case Fatality Rate (2026 BDBV)
value: ~48.3% (DRC, crude, as of 13 Sept); ~62.2% in North Kivu province (as of 13 Sept)
source: ECDC Ebola outbreak tracker (published 15 September) — data as of 13 September 2026
contestNote: Crude national CFR calculated from reported confirmed cases/deaths; DRC's overall CFR has climbed from roughly 20% in early June to a peak near 48.6% in late August and stood at roughly 48.3% as of 13 September (7,258 cases / 3,510 deaths). Province-level variation remains stark: North Kivu (1,281 cases / 797 deaths as of 13 September) sits near 62.2%, well above the national average, which responders and outside experts attribute to weaker treatment access rather than a change in virus behavior. Africa CDC warned 22 August that if the official case count captures only 30-40% of true infections, the true CFR could be substantially lower than the crude reported figure. BDBV historically 25–47% CFR; this outbreak's crude national CFR now sits at or above the top of the historical range.

label: BDBV Vaccine Status — ~2,000 Frontline Workers Vaccinated of 50,000 Target; Phase 3 Trial Still Slated for October/November
value: ~2,000 of 70,000 allocated Ervebo doses administered to frontline/health workers in Tshopo and Bas-Uélé (target 50,000); 20,000 doses reserved for the Phase 3 trial, still targeted for October or November
source: WHO / Africa CDC / ICG / Healio / medicalxpress — 12 August–10 September 2026
contestNote: 20 August: WHO and Africa CDC announced the ICG approved immediate release of 70,000 Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV) doses to DRC — 20,000 for a Phase 3 clinical trial testing cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus, 50,000 for frontline and health workers. WHO said 10 September that roughly 2,000 frontline and health workers, stationed in Tshopo and Bas-Uélé provinces, have received Ervebo under the compassionate-use campaign DRC launched 27 August, still far short of the 50,000-dose target. WHO cautioned 'it is not known whether Ervebo may be protective against the Bundibugyo virus in humans,' though early lab/animal data suggest possible partial protection. WHO vaccines chief Kate O'Brien said 2 September the Phase 3 trial 'should begin by October or November,' with Ervebo likely first into the trial given its existing licensure; medicalxpress confirmed 10 September the timeline remains October/November, with the trial to be implemented in Ituri by a consortium including DRC's INRB, CEPI, the Institute of Tropical Medicine (Belgium), MSF and Africa CDC. Tedros noted two additional candidates (Oxford's ChAdOx1 BDBV in the UK and a Moderna mRNA candidate in Canada) remain in earlier-stage safety trials.
delta: ~2,000 doses administered under compassionate use since the 27 August campaign launch, reported 10 September
deltaNote: The 28 May WHO expert panel ruling barred Ervebo use outside research settings; the 7 August TAG-CVP recommendation, 12 August trial talks, 20 August dose allocation, 27 August compassionate-use campaign launch, and the confirmed October/November trial target are successive steps toward a structured clinical trial pathway alongside limited frontline-worker protection. Since the ICG mechanism's 2021 establishment, over 56,000 Ervebo doses have been allocated for DRC outbreaks combined, plus 167,000 doses in preventive campaigns across five countries.

label: DRC Provinces + Countries Affected
value: 62 of 167 health zones across 7 DRC provinces + Uganda (outbreak closed) + France (recovered) + Germany (treated)
source: ECDC Ebola Outbreak Tracker (data as of 13 September) — published 15 September 2026
delta: Health-zone count held at 62 of 167 across all seven provinces (Ituri 28/36, North Kivu 16/34, Tshopo 7/23, Haut-Uélé 6/13, Bas-Uélé 3/11, South Kivu 1/34, Sud-Ubangi 1/16); DRC Health Minister Roger Samuel Kamba said 10 of the 62 zones had gone 22+ days without a new case, calling it 'a positive signal' that the response 'is beginning to bend the transmission curve' — a claim UN and WHO officials said 15 September was too early to confirm as a peak
deltaNote: Ituri Province remains the epicenter with the large majority of cases and deaths across 28 of 36 health zones. North Kivu (16 of 34 zones, including Katwa, Biena and Manguredjipa) has the highest fatality rate of any affected province and, per Africa CDC's Yap Boum, drove much of the outbreak's growth through early September; officials link the acceleration to M23/government force fighting around Goma. Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uélé round out the six eastern provinces; Sud-Ubangi (first case 9 September, first in western DRC, bordering the Central African Republic and Republic of Congo) is now folded into the 167-zone denominator. Sud-Ubangi's acting governor Jean-René Galekwa Vundawe said 38 contacts of the index patient have been quarantined. Ebola cases were also detected among schoolchildren in Bunia, Ituri, as the 2026-27 school year opened in early September. Uganda's outbreak (Kampala + Wakiso) was declared over by its own Ministry of Health on 28 July and confirmed over by WHO on 25 August after the 42-day monitoring period. Mambasa Territory (IS-controlled) remains largely inaccessible to response teams. WHO's second IHR Emergency Committee meeting (24 August) maintained PHEIC status and expanded 'high risk' guidance to nine bordering states including Burundi and the Central African Republic.

label: Contact Tracing Coverage (DRC)
source: ECDC Ebola outbreak tracker — data as of 13 September 2026 (published 15 September)
delta: National coverage fell sharply to 78.6% (13 September) from 88% (12 September)
deltaNote: The 13 September update put active follow-up at 78.6% of identified contacts nationally, a nine-point drop from the 88% reported 12 September. WHO's 100-day assessment noted tracing coverage had climbed dramatically from just 9% in the outbreak's first week, but the metric has fluctuated week to week (85.7% on 5 Sept → 88.3% on 7 Sept → 84.4% on 9 Sept → 88% on 12 Sept → 78.6% on 13 Sept) as the outbreak's geographic footprint keeps expanding, most recently to a seventh province (Sud-Ubangi) via a single patient's roughly three-week, multi-province journey. A recalibrated Lancet Infectious Diseases modelling study put the probability of Ebola spillover into South Sudan at roughly 69.3%, prompting a WHO/UNMISS preparedness mission to the border town of Ezo (27-28 August); no confirmed South Sudan case has been reported as of 13 September. Uganda's contact-tracing program is closed following its outbreak-end declaration, confirmed by WHO on 25 August. Mambasa Territory (IS-controlled) remains a contact-tracing dead zone, and community resistance (isolation refusals, a patient escape in Katwa, blocked ring-closure in Tshopo) is separately undermining follow-up in several provinces. UN Special Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis said 15 September the response gap is widening in North Kivu, where weekly cases have doubled from roughly 100 to 200.
